comparison.correct: Press the last E on 3 and hold it through 4.
comparison.tempting: Press E on both 3 and 4 to finish the phrase.
comparison.why: The written ending is one two-beat note. Pressing again on 4 adds an attack; keeping the key down preserves the intended rhythm.

first.anchor: Put three fingers over the route
first.prompt: Which finger starts the first E?
first.hint: Your thumb is waiting over C.
first.help: Middle finger starts E; index takes D; thumb takes C. Keep those three keys under the hand rather than reaching for each note.

first.prompt: What happens after the thumb plays C?
first.hint: The first group turns back upward.
first.help: Return to D with the index. Practise only D–C–D if the thumb makes you pause; keep all three starts equally spaced.

first.prompt: What does the finger do on the final 4?
first.hint: A count does not always need a new press.
first.help: Keep the last E down on 4. You already started it on 3. Release at the following 1, after both counted beats have passed.

first.prompt: How can seven presses fill eight beats?
first.hint: Compare the last note with the six earlier notes.
first.help: Six notes use one beat each; the last uses two: 6 + 2 = 8. The extra beat belongs to the held sound, not a pause after it.

second.prompt: Which two notes sit immediately across the join?
second.hint: Use the last note before the bar line and the first after it.
second.help: D ends the first four-note group; E starts the next. E–D–C alone never reaches that handover, so it cannot practise the join.

second.anchor: Keep a note on either side of the join
second.prompt: Does the bar line add a pause?
second.hint: Say 3, 4, 1, 2 evenly.
second.help: No. The count returns to 1 without inserting time. C–D | E–E occupies four equal beats, even though it crosses into a new bar.

second.prompt: What speed should you use when restoring the full phrase?
second.hint: Keep the speed that worked for the small fragment.
second.help: Use the same slow tempo. Making the surrounding notes faster brings back the rushed join you just repaired.

second.prompt: When should the last E release?
second.hint: Beat 4 still belongs to the last E.
second.help: Release at the next 1. Releasing as you say 4 cuts off half of the two-beat note, even if the earlier join is even.

comparison.correct: E4–G4–C5 together is C major with E in the bass.
comparison.tempting: E4–G4–C5 must be E major because E is lowest.
comparison.why: The three note names are C, E and G, so the chord is still C major. E is its bass here; it does not become the root just by sounding lowest.

first.anchor: Locate C before placing the other fingers
first.prompt: Which note gives this chord its name?
first.hint: Start with the root specified in the problem.
first.help: C names this C-major chord. The 4 in C4 identifies the register. It is not a chord number or a finger instruction.

first.prompt: Does “third” mean three semitone steps?
first.hint: Count letters once, then inspect keyboard distances separately.
first.help: No. C–D–E makes E the third letter counted from C. The distance C to E is four semitones; those are two different kinds of counting.

first.prompt: What stays fixed when you hear the arpeggio?
first.hint: Compare the note names with the block chord.
first.help: C4, E4 and G4 stay fixed. Only their starting times are separated. Do not add D or F just because the fingers pass over them.

first.anchor: Give all three notes one beginning
first.prompt: What must be prepared before a shared start?
first.hint: Put the three fingers over their keys first.
first.help: Locate C, E and G before pressing. Otherwise the hand may search while playing, producing an accidental arpeggio instead of a block chord.

second.prompt: Which single note moved from the original shape?
second.hint: Compare C4–E4–G4 with E4–G4–C5.
second.help: The lower C became the higher C. E4 and G4 stayed where they were. The note name C remains in the chord.

second.prompt: What is the difference between bass and root here?
second.hint: One names a sounding position; the other identifies the chord.
second.help: E4 is the lowest sound, so it is the bass. C is the root of the C-major chord even though the C is now on top.

second.anchor: Name the chord and its arrangement
second.prompt: Why is the chord not E major?
second.hint: List the actual note names before using the lowest note as a label.
second.help: The notes are E, G and C. E major would contain E, G-sharp and B. Moving C above the other tones did not supply those notes.

second.prompt: Can an inversion also be an arpeggio?
second.hint: Arrangement and starting times answer different questions.
second.help: Yes. E–G–C is first inversion because E is lowest. Play those tones in succession and you have an arpeggio of that inversion.

comparison.correct: Trabajo por la mañana y estudio por la noche.
comparison.tempting: Trabajas por la mañana y estudias por la noche means I work and study.
comparison.why: For these regular verbs, the as forms address a familiar you. The o forms trabajo and estudio express I in the intended routine.

first.prompt: What do you change in trabajar to say I work?
first.hint: Keep trabaj- and choose the I ending.
first.help: Remove ar, not the whole last syllable of the stem. Trabaj- plus o gives trabajo. Adding o to trabajar would leave the infinitive ending in place.

first.prompt: Why is estudio enough without yo?
first.hint: The verb ending already helps identify the speaker.
first.help: Here estudio expresses I study. Yo estudio is also grammatical; the explicit pronoun can add contrast, but you do not need it in every sentence.

first.anchor: Place each action in the day
first.prompt: Which words keep the meaning in the morning?
first.hint: Read the whole phrase, not just mañana.
first.help: Por la mañana gives the time of day here. Mañana trabajo instead means I work tomorrow. Use the complete phrase when practising the routine.

first.prompt: Do the verbs change when you add y?
first.hint: You are joining two complete statements.
first.help: No. Trabajo stays trabajo and estudio stays estudio. Y simply connects the information; it does not introduce a new person.

second.prompt: Who is comes about in this question?
second.hint: You are asking one friend.
second.help: Comes is the familiar you form of comer. Como is the I form, so swapping in como would change who the eating is about.

second.prompt: What part of vivir stays in vivo?
second.hint: Remove the infinitive ending ir.
second.help: Viv- remains; add o for I. Vivo cerca says where you live without saying that you live in the friend’s house.

second.prompt: Why do comes and vivo have different endings?
second.hint: The subject changes between the two lines.
second.help: The question is about you, the friend; the statement is about me, the speaker. Do not choose endings merely by copying the previous line.

second.anchor: Keep the answer suited to the question
second.prompt: Does Vivo cerca directly answer whether you eat at home?
second.hint: Nearby describes a location, not an eating habit.
second.help: No. You can add Sí, como en casa as the direct answer. Vivo cerca supplies different information and may follow it as an extra detail.

comparison.correct: La reunión es en la oficina gives the meeting’s venue.
comparison.tempting: La reunión must use está because its location is temporary.
comparison.why: A meeting’s venue is commonly expressed with ser: La reunión es en la oficina. Whether that meeting lasts an hour or a day does not turn this into the person-location pattern.

first.anchor: Say what you want the friend to understand
first.prompt: Which meaning are you trying to express?
first.hint: Separate feeling bored from being boring to someone else.
first.help: You want the feeling: I have nothing interesting to do. That directs you to estoy aburrido or estoy aburrida in this model.

first.prompt: Does aburrida change the feeling into a different meaning?
first.hint: Compare only the adjective’s o and a endings.
first.help: No. Estoy aburrido and estoy aburrida both mean I am bored. The ending matches the speaker; the verb remains estoy in both.

first.anchor: Change only the verb and listen again
first.prompt: What changes when estoy becomes soy?
first.hint: Keep the adjective fixed for this comparison.
first.help: The usual reading changes from I am bored to I am boring. This is a change of meaning, not a stopwatch marking how long boredom lasts.

first.prompt: Would a long wait make soy the right choice for bored?
first.hint: The intended message has not changed.
first.help: No. The phrase for feeling bored still uses estoy here. Duration is not a reliable way to choose between these two expressions.

second.prompt: What is being located in Estoy en la oficina?
second.hint: Read the subject carried by estoy.
second.help: The speaker is at the office. Estoy is I am in this estar pattern; en la oficina tells you where.

second.prompt: What does La reunión es en la oficina tell you?
second.hint: A meeting is an event, and this sentence supplies its venue.
second.help: It says where the meeting takes place. Learn es en la oficina with that event meaning rather than forcing the person-location pattern onto it.

second.prompt: Why does the same office not require the same verb?
second.hint: Compare the subjects and messages, not only the place phrase.
second.help: One sentence locates me; the other states where an event takes place. Sharing en la oficina does not erase that distinction.

second.prompt: Does temporary versus permanent explain both sentences?
second.hint: Both could be true for only one afternoon.
second.help: No. I can be at the office briefly and the meeting can also be brief. The two constructions still use estoy and es respectively.

comparison.correct: Be3 blocks the rook’s checking line to e1.
comparison.tempting: Bd2 answers the check because it is a valid bishop diagonal.
comparison.why: D2 is not on the checking e-file. E3 is. The resulting attack on the king, not just the bishop’s move shape, determines whether the reply is legal.

first.prompt: Which attack must the next move remove?
first.hint: Trace the rook’s file all the way to the king.
first.help: The rook on e8 attacks e1 through six empty squares. White cannot ignore that present attack by making an unrelated developing move.

first.prompt: Why does Bd2 fail despite being a diagonal move?
first.hint: Look at the rook’s line after placing the bishop on d2.
first.help: D2 is off the e-file. The move obeys the bishop’s movement pattern but still leaves White’s king attacked, making it illegal.

first.anchor: Place the bishop on the attack line
first.prompt: What changes when the bishop lands on e3?
first.hint: E3 lies between the checking rook and the king.
first.help: The rook no longer has a clear path to e1. Blocking works against this sliding attack because the bishop physically interrupts its line.

first.prompt: Why must you inspect more than the checking rook?
first.hint: Removing one attack would not remove a second attacker.
first.help: Check every black piece after the candidate move. Here the king on a8 does not attack White’s king, so blocking the rook removes the only check.

second.anchor: Find the target of the diagonal
second.prompt: Which white piece is actually attacked by Bd4?
second.hint: Follow d4–c3–b2–a1.
second.help: That diagonal ends at the rook on a1. The king is on h1, a different square. A threat to a rook is not automatically check.

second.prompt: Does Bd4 attack the white king on h1?
second.hint: Trace the bishop’s other downward diagonal too.
second.help: It reaches e3, f2 and g1, not h1. With Black’s king far away on h8, White is not in check in this stated position.

second.prompt: Why is a2 a useful rook destination here?
second.hint: Inspect both enemy pieces from the new square.
second.help: A2 is off the bishop’s diagonals from d4 and outside the black king’s reach. Ra2 moves the rook out of attack without exposing the king.

second.anchor: Check what your move leaves behind
second.prompt: Does an attacked rook always have to move?
second.hint: The legal requirement concerns your king; saving material is a choice.
second.help: No. You may have another useful capture or forcing move in another position. Here Ra2 is simply one verified way to save this rook.

comparison.correct: Bxa8 is a legal reply, so the original rook-check position is not mate.
comparison.tempting: No safe king move means the rook-check position is checkmate.
comparison.why: White’s bishop can capture the checking rook on a8. The search must include replies by every white piece, not only destinations of the king.

first.prompt: What makes this a check before White moves?
first.hint: Use the rook’s file, not the king’s lack of space.
first.help: The rook on a8 has an open path to a1. A king can have few squares without being in check; here a specific rook attack establishes it.

first.anchor: Rule out the king’s three destinations
first.prompt: Have you disproved every reply after testing the king?
first.hint: White still has a bishop.
first.help: No. You have ruled out king moves only. Look at whether the bishop can capture the attacker or block the attack before calling mate.

first.anchor: Let another piece remove the attacker
first.prompt: Why is Bxa8 a legal response?
first.hint: Remove the rook, then inspect what can still attack a1.
first.help: The bishop reaches a8 diagonally and captures the rook. The remaining black king on c2 is not adjacent to a1, so the checking attack is gone.

first.anchor: Use the one legal reply to decide
first.prompt: How many legal replies must you find to disprove mate?
first.hint: Mate means there are none.
first.help: One is enough. Bxa8 gives a counterexample to the claim that no legal reply exists; you do not need every other defence to work.

second.anchor: Ask whether the king’s current square is attacked
second.prompt: Does Qb6 attack a8?
second.hint: Compare the file and rank differences.
second.help: No. A8 is one file left and two ranks above b6. A queen needs the same file, same rank or equal file-and-rank change for a diagonal.

second.prompt: Why is a7 unsafe even though a8 is safe?
second.hint: A7 and a8 have different relationships to Qb6.
second.help: A7 is diagonally adjacent to b6, so the queen attacks it. A8 is not on that diagonal. Check a destination independently of the starting square.

second.anchor: Inspect b7 and b8, then look for another piece
second.prompt: Could another black piece move instead?
second.hint: Read the full stated position.
second.help: No: Black has only its king. B7 and b8 are queen-attacked, a7 is queen-attacked, and there is no other black piece that could move.

second.anchor: Combine no check with no legal move
second.prompt: Why is the result a draw rather than a win by mate?
second.hint: Bring back the first finding: no check.
second.help: Black has no legal move, but its king is not attacked. Under standard rules that combination is stalemate, which draws the game.
